author: reek
body: A runnable model of screen-space reflections with a GGX weighting. A reflective point goes in, the colour arriving along its reflected direction comes out.

author: reek
body: Screen-space reflection is not a way of computing reflections. It is a way of REUSING a frame that has already been drawn: the reflected ray is marched against the depth buffer of the image on screen, and where it crosses a surface, the colour already sitting in the framebuffer at that pixel is the answer. That is the whole trick, and it is why it is cheap enough to be everywhere in real-time rendering.

author: reek
body: Two screen-sized buffers in guest RAM below the framebuffer: one distance per pixel and one packed normal. The colour buffer is the framebuffer itself, which is the entire point -- SSR samples the image it is part of.

author: reek
body: Depth is stored as the bit pattern of a single-precision Real rather than as a fixed-point integer. `real-approx-to-bits` and `bits-to-real-approx` are exact inverses, so the buffer holds the distance the march actually computed and not a quantised version of it, and a 32-bit cell holds it without a second word. A fixed-point encoding would have had to choose a range and a precision, and both would have been wrong somewhere.

author: reek
body: The normal packs into three bytes with the material flag in the fourth, so one 32-bit cell carries everything the reflection pass needs to know about a pixel. A byte per axis is about half a degree of angular resolution, which is far finer than a reflection off a rough surface can show.

author: reek
body: Clearing the depth buffer to a negative distance is what makes "nothing was drawn here" a value the march can test rather than a state it has to infer. Zero would not do: zero is a legal distance.

author: reek
body: The camera basis, and the projection that turns a world point back into the pixel it was drawn at. The march needs this every step, and it is the hinge the whole technique turns on: without a projection there is no way to ask the depth buffer about a world position.

author: reek
body: The mirror direction. Everything else here is bookkeeping; this is the physics.

author: reek
body: The edge fade. A reflection that runs off the side of the screen has to go somewhere, and stopping it abruptly draws a hard line along the border that reads as a rendering error. Fading it out over a margin turns the failure into something that looks like a reflection falling off with distance, which is the conventional lie and a convincing one.

author: reek
body: One step of the march. The test is the crossing test that defines SSR: the sample is behind the surface the depth buffer recorded for that pixel.

author: reek
body: What decides it is the SIGN CHANGE between consecutive samples. If the ray was in front of the recorded surface and is now behind it, it crossed that surface somewhere in between, whatever the depths involved. The thickness bound survives, demoted to what it should always have been: a guard against a step so coarse that the crossing tells us nothing, rather than the test itself.

author: reek
body: The march, and the thing that makes this SCREEN-space rather than a world march that happens to consult a depth buffer.

author: reek
body: The first version here stepped through the world and projected each sample. It works looking down at water and falls apart looking across it, which is exactly the view worth rendering: at grazing incidence the reflected ray runs nearly parallel to the surface, so a world-space step of fixed length crawls across the screen in some places and leaps whole mountains in others. Hits become erratic, and the reflection comes out as salt-and-pepper noise rather than an image. Measured on this scene, that version found a hit on 15% of water pixels and the hits it found were scattered.

author: reek
body: Stepping in screen space fixes it by construction. The ray's endpoints are projected once, and the march walks the straight line BETWEEN THEM at a fixed stride in pixels, so no pixel on the ray's path is skipped and none is visited twice, whatever the angle. Depth comes along by interpolating its reciprocal, which is linear in screen space for a straight world ray and is the reason `pz` is view-axis depth.

author: reek
body: A floor on the step count, and it is not the same criterion as the stride. The stride exists so no PIXEL on the ray's path is skipped; this exists so no DEPTH is. A reflected ray running nearly parallel to the water projects both its endpoints close together near the horizon, so the pixel span is short and the stride rule asks for a handful of steps -- while that same short span covers kilometres of world distance. The crossing then falls between samples and is missed, which is the grazing case this whole scene consists of.

author: reek
body: `reject` names a material flag the march refuses to strike. It exists because a reflective surface must not reflect ITSELF: the second-order reflection that would require is not in the frame, and accepting the crossing anyway samples the reflecting surface's own colour, which on water reads as bright flecks scattered along every shallow contact. Real implementations exclude the source surface for the same reason. Passing zero rejects nothing.

author: reek
body: The endpoint is clamped in front of the camera rather than projected blindly: a reflected ray that passes behind the eye has no screen-space line at all, and shortening it until it does is what keeps the march defined for rays that leave the frustum sideways.

author: reek
body: Roughness perturbs the reflected direction. One sample, not a cone: a proper GGX importance sample would take many rays per pixel and this model takes one, so what it produces is a noisy estimate of the same integral rather than a smooth one. Saying so is better than implying a blur that is not there.
